newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir's new chief minister calls for peace.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir's new chief minister calls for peace.

text.p: The new chief minister of India's Jammu and Kashmir state on Friday appealed to separatist guerrillas to give up their arms and help bring back peace to the troubled state.

"I invite all those misled youth who still carry weapons that they should give up their arms, come forward and join the national mainstream to contribute in the reconstruction of a Naya Kashmir (new Kashmir)," Farooq Abdullah said in his first radio address to the people of the Himalayan state.
"If they (separatists) move a step forward, we would move two steps towards them for friendship," he said.
Dozens of separatist groups in Kashmir are fighting for independence or for closer ties with neighbouring Pakistan. They boycotted recent polls, calling them a "mockery of Kashmiri aspirations".
More than 20,000 people have been killed since a separatist revolt began in Kashmir in 1990, hospitals and police sources say.

Abdullah took office as chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state on Wednesday after nearly seven years of federal rule. On Friday morning, he delivered his radio address in Urdu, the official language of India's only Moslem majority state.
Abdullah said the newly elected government of the region would set up a commission to monitor human rights violations.

"We will impose a ban on violation of human rights, for which a human rights commission will be constituted shortly. This commission will take an adequate notice of human rights violations and the guilty will be punished," Abdullah said.
"Innocents or those with the least charges will be released," he added.
International human rights groups have accused India of grave human rights violations in Kashmir, but the government has denied the allegations.
Abdullah said violence would not break the state's relationship with the Indian union.
"The stability and longevity of this relationship with the Indian union is beneficient to Jammu and Kashmir," Abdullah said.
Jammu and Kashmir's accession to India after independence from the British in 1947 provided autonomy to the state, which was envisaged in the Indian constitution, Abdullah said.
Abdullah's National Conference comfortably won the elections last month on a promise by India's federal government that autonomy would be granted.
India's constitution gave Kashmiris control over most affairs, but New Delhi has since 1952 gradually eroded these powers. Abdullah wants to restore them.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda has pledged "maximum autonomy" to Jammu and Kashmir.

"Now the state has elected its representative government, I hope that New Delhi will fulfill its promise on autonomy for which representatives of both the Indian and Jammu and Kashmir governments will have to initiate negotiations soon," the new chief minister said.
